core.h: Locus of a Moving Point Under Constraints
core.p: Advanced OCR questions combine loci with boat navigation, animal tethering, or sprinkler coverage. You must handle boundary transitions smoothly.
bullets: A goat tethered by a rope of length L to the corner of a shed sweeps out circular sectors.
If the rope wraps around the corner of a fence or wall, the radius of the arc changes at the pivot point.
Intersection of multiple loci defines the exact landing zone or valid movement corridor.
Always write down scale conversions if the map uses a ratio like 1cm : 5m.

callouts.p: When a tethered animal hits a fence corner, the fence post becomes the new centre of rotation for the next arc segment.

analogy.t: The Treasure Map and Surveyor's Stakes
analogy.p: Imagine you are burying treasure on an island. One rule says 'stay within 50 paces of the old oak tree' (a circular fence around a point). Another rule says 'stay closer to the stone pillar than the iron statue' (a fence built along the perpendicular bisector line). The region where you can legally walk without breaking either rule is the intersection of these zones. The analogy breaks down because real terrain has bumps and obstacles, whereas geometric loci assume a perfectly flat Euclidean plane.

terms.d: A set of points that share a specified geometric property or rule.
A line dividing a line segment into two equal parts at a 90-degree angle.
A line dividing an angle into two equal halves.
At exactly equal distances from two or more objects.
A curved part of the circumference of a circle used in constructions.
The point where two line segments or rays meet to form an angle.
A ruler with no measurement markings used solely for drawing straight lines.
A V-shaped instrument with one pointy leg and one pencil leg used for drawing circles and arcs.
An area bounded by one or more locus lines satisfying certain inequalities.
A condition using < or > represented by a dashed construction boundary.
A condition using <= or >= represented by a solid construction boundary.
A rope or chain limiting the movement of a point object around a fixed anchor.
Intersecting at or forming right angles (90 degrees).
The exact point where lines, arcs, or loci cross each other.

mistakes.w: Erasing construction arcs after finishing the drawing
mistakes.r: Leave all arcs visible; examiners deduct marks if construction lines are missing.

mistakes.w: Using a protractor to measure angles in construction questions
mistakes.r: Constructions must be done strictly using a ruler and compasses only.

mistakes.w: Drawing a straight line for a locus of a fixed distance from a point
mistakes.r: A fixed distance from a single point is always a circle, not straight lines.

mistakes.w: Shading the wrong side of a perpendicular bisector when asked for the region closer to B
mistakes.r: Shade the side containing B, verified by testing a point.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the semi-circular ends when drawing the locus of a fixed distance from a line segment
mistakes.r: Include semicircles of radius r centred on endpoints A and B.

mistakes.w: Changing the compass width randomly while bisecting a line
mistakes.r: Keep the compass width constant greater than half length AB for both arcs.

exam.q: Construct the perpendicular bisector of line AB. Leave in all your construction arcs.
model: Arc centres at A and B with equal radius greater than half AB
Accurate perpendicular bisector line drawn intersecting both pairs of arcs
exam.tip: Make sure your compass opening is noticeably more than half the length of AB.

exam.q: Bisect angle XYZ using a ruler and compasses.
model: Arc drawn from vertex Y cutting both arms XY and YZ
Intersecting arcs drawn from arm intersection points, with angle bisector line through Y
exam.tip: Ensure the arc from vertex Y crosses both arms clearly.

exam.q: Shade the region that is closer to point A than point B, and within 4cm of point A.
model: Perpendicular bisector of AB constructed accurately
Circle of radius 4cm centred at A drawn accurately
Correct side of perpendicular bisector shaded
Inside of 4cm circle shaded, identifying the exact overlapping region
exam.tip: Do not shade until all boundary lines and circles are fully drawn.

exam.q: Construct a 60 degree angle at point P on a baseline.
model: Arc of fixed radius drawn from P intersecting baseline
Arc of same radius drawn from baseline intersection crossing first arc, connected to P
exam.tip: This forms an equilateral triangle of side length equal to your compass radius.

exam.q: A goat is tied to corner C of a rectangular shed measuring 4m by 6m by a rope of length 5m. Draw the locus of the goat's outer boundary.
model: Quarter circle of radius 5m centred at C
Arcs adjusting where the rope hits the adjacent walls of length 1m and 3m
Complete continuous outer boundary curve shown
exam.tip: Watch out for the rope wrapping around corners when the length exceeds the wall dimensions.

exam.q: Construct the perpendicular from point P to the straight line AB.
model: Arc centred at P cutting line AB at two points
Intersecting arcs drawn below AB from those two points, line dropped from P
exam.tip: Ensure your arcs below the line cross cleanly to give an exact point.

exam.q: Shade the region that is less than 3cm from line AB and closer to A than B.
model: Parallel boundary lines 3cm from AB with semicircles at ends
Correct region satisfying both inequalities shaded clearly
exam.tip: Label your regions lightly in pencil before final shading if needed.

exam.q: Construct a 30 degree angle using a ruler and compasses.
model: Bisect the 60 degree angle using compasses
Accurate straight line drawn for the 30 degree ray
exam.tip: Never measure with a protractor; build it up from standard constructions.

worked.q: Construct the perpendicular bisector of a line segment PQ of length 8cm and use it to find a point X on the bisector that is 6cm from the midpoint.
steps: Draw a straight line segment PQ of length 8cm using a ruler.
Place the compass point on P, open it to 6cm (greater than half of 8cm), and draw arcs above and below the line.
Without changing the compass width, place the compass point on Q and draw intersecting arcs above and below PQ.
Join the two arc intersections with a straight line to form the perpendicular bisector.
Measure 6cm along the bisector from the midpoint of PQ and label that point X.
worked.ans: Accurate perpendicular bisector with visible construction arcs and point X marked 6cm from the midpoint.

worked.q: A treasure chest is buried in a field. It is equidistant from trees A and B, and exactly 5m from fence line CD. Using a scale of 1cm to 1m, construct the possible positions for the chest.
steps: Draw trees A and B and fence line CD according to the 1cm:1m scale.
Construct the perpendicular bisector between A and B.
Construct parallel boundary lines 5cm away from fence line CD on both sides.
Identify the points where the perpendicular bisector intersects the 5cm parallel boundary lines.
worked.ans: The possible positions are the exact intersection points of the perpendicular bisector and the 5cm parallel lines.

maths_ocr_h.7.5.summary: Understanding 3D geometry involves categorizing solids by their properties—faces, edges, and vertices—and accurately representing these objects in two dimensions. Mastery of plans, elevations, and nets is essential for spatial reasoning, allowing students to translate between complex 3D structures and their orthographic projections, which is a fundamental skill in engineering and architecture. Grade 9 students must be able to move fluently between 3D visualisations and 2D representations, including the use of hidden lines and isometric grids.

core.p: A polyhedron is a 3D shape with flat faces, straight edges, and sharp corners (vertices). Understanding the relationship between these components is the foundation of 3D geometry.
bullets: **Face**: A flat surface of a 3D shape.
**Edge**: The line segment where two faces meet.
**Vertex**: A point where three or more edges meet (plural: vertices).
**Euler's Formula**: For any convex polyhedron, V - E + F = 2, where V is vertices, E is edges, and F is faces.

callouts.p: A solid figure with many flat faces, typically more than six.

core.p: Prisms are a specific class of polyhedra defined by their uniformity along their length. While a cylinder shares properties with a prism, it is not a polyhedron because it has curved surfaces.
bullets: **Prism**: A solid with a constant cross-section throughout its length.
**Cross-section**: The shape formed by cutting through a solid at right angles to its axis.
**Cylinder**: Has two circular ends joined by a curved surface; it is essentially a 'circular prism'.
The number of faces in an n-gonal prism is always n + 2.

core.p: Pyramids and cones taper from a base to a single point called the apex. The properties change based on the shape of the base.
bullets: **Pyramid**: A polyhedron with a polygonal base and triangular faces that meet at an apex.
**Cone**: Has a circular base and a curved surface tapering to an apex.
**Tetrahedron**: A triangular-based pyramid; it is the simplest polyhedron with 4 faces, 4 vertices, and 6 edges.

fig.cap: A square-based pyramid showing the relationship between the base, the triangular faces, and the apex.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><path d="M100 180 L300 180 L340 140 L140 140 Z" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M100 180 L220 40 L300 180" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M340 140 L220 40 L140 140" fill="none" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="210" y="30" fill="#1b2540">Apex</text><text x="180" y="210" fill="#1b2540">Square Base</text><text x="280" y="100" fill="#1b2540">Slant Face</text></svg>

core.p: There are only five regular polyhedra, known as Platonic solids, where every face is an identical regular polygon and the same number of faces meet at each vertex.
bullets: **Tetrahedron**: 4 faces (triangles).
**Cube (Hexahedron)**: 6 faces (squares).
**Octahedron**: 8 faces (triangles).
**Dodecahedron**: 12 faces (pentagons).
**Icosahedron**: 20 faces (triangles).

callouts.p: In a Platonic solid, all faces, edges, and angles are congruent.

core.p: Orthographic projection is the method of representing a 3D object by three 2D drawings from specific viewpoints.
bullets: **Plan**: The view from directly above the object.
**Front Elevation**: The view from the front of the object.
**Side Elevation**: The view from one side (usually specified as left or right).

callouts.p: Always check the orientation. The 'Front' is often indicated by an arrow on the 3D diagram.

core.p: When drawing these, you must project the dimensions accurately. The width of the front elevation must match the width of the plan.
bullets: Use a sharp pencil and a ruler.
Draw on the grid provided (usually 1cm squared paper).
**Hidden Lines**: Use dashed lines to indicate edges that exist but are hidden from that specific viewpoint.
Ensure the height of the front elevation matches the height of the side elevation.

fig.cap: Orthographic projections of an L-shaped block. Note how the dimensions align across the plan and elevations.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="40" y="40" width="60" height="60" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540"/><rect x="40" y="100" width="120" height="60" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="40" y="30" fill="#1b2540">Plan View</text><rect x="220" y="100" width="120" height="60" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540"/><line x1="280" y1="100" x2="280" y2="160" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-dasharray="4"/><text x="220" y="90" fill="#1b2540">Front Elevation</text><rect x="220" y="180" width="60" height="40" fill="#fecaca" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="220" y="175" fill="#1b2540">Side Elevation</text></svg>

core.p: A net is a 2D pattern that can be folded to form a 3D solid. Visualising how faces connect is key to solving net problems.
bullets: A cube has 11 possible nets.
The net of a cylinder consists of two circles and one rectangle.
The length of the rectangle in a cylinder's net is equal to the circumference of the circular base (C = 2 * pi * r).
The net of a cone is a sector of a circle plus a smaller circle for the base.

fig.cap: The net of a cylinder. The width of the rectangle must equal the circumference of the circles to fold correctly.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="100" y="80" width="200" height="80" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540"/><circle cx="200" cy="40" r="40" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540"/><circle cx="200" cy="200" r="40" fill="#e9d5ff" stroke="#1b2540"/><text x="110" y="125" fill="#1b2540">Circumference Length</text><text x="310" y="125" fill="#1b2540">Height</text></svg>

core.p: Isometric paper uses a grid of dots forming equilateral triangles. It allows you to draw 3D objects where vertical lines remain vertical, and horizontal lines are drawn at 30 degrees.
bullets: Parallel lines on the object remain parallel on the drawing.
There is no perspective (objects do not get smaller as they get further away).
Useful for translating plans and elevations back into a 3D form.

callouts.p: Do not draw horizontal lines on isometric paper; they must follow the 30-degree grid lines.

core.p: Spheres are unique as they have no edges or vertices, only one continuous curved face.
bullets: A sphere looks like a circle from every elevation and the plan.
A hemisphere has two faces: one flat circular base and one curved surface.
A hemisphere has 1 edge (the boundary of the base) and 0 vertices.

core.p: OCR Higher papers often feature shapes made of multiple cuboids or prisms. You must be able to calculate total faces, edges, and vertices for these.
bullets: When two shapes are joined, some faces are 'lost' inside the join.
The number of vertices may decrease if they coincide.
Always count carefully, marking off faces as you go to avoid double-counting.

analogy.p: Imagine a 3D shape is a house. The 'Plan' is what a bird sees flying directly over the roof. The 'Elevations' are what a person sees standing directly in front of the house or at the side. You need all three views to build the house correctly; a single view might hide a secret extension or a chimney. The 'Net' is like the cardboard box the house came in, flattened out. The analogy breaks down because real buildings have internal walls and thickness, whereas in GCSE geometry, we usually treat solids as 'filled' or focus only on the external surface boundaries.

mistakes.w: Drawing the plan and elevations with different scales.
mistakes.r: Ensure the width of the front elevation and the width of the plan are identical.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to use dashed lines for hidden edges.
mistakes.r: Always use dashed lines for edges that are obscured from view but exist.

mistakes.w: Assuming a cylinder net is just two circles and any rectangle.
mistakes.r: The rectangle's length must exactly equal the circumference of the circle.

mistakes.w: Miscounting vertices on a prism.
mistakes.r: Remember a prism has 2n vertices, where n is the number of sides of the base.

mistakes.w: Drawing horizontal lines on isometric paper.
mistakes.r: All 'horizontal' lines must be drawn at a 30-degree angle along the grid dots.

mistakes.w: Confusing a pyramid with a prism.
mistakes.r: A prism has a constant cross-section; a pyramid tapers to a point.

mistakes.w: Thinking a sphere has one vertex (the top).
mistakes.r: A sphere has zero vertices and zero edges.

mistakes.w: Neglecting the 'Front' arrow in exam diagrams.
mistakes.r: The arrow defines which view is the 'Front Elevation'; ignore it and you lose marks.

exam.q: A prism has a cross-section of a regular pentagon. How many faces, edges, and vertices does it have?
exam.tip: For an n-sided prism: Faces = n+2, Edges = 3n, Vertices = 2n.

exam.q: Draw the plan of a sphere with radius 3cm.
model: A circle with a radius of 3cm (or diameter 6cm).
exam.tip: Spheres look like circles from every orthographic direction.

exam.q: Verify Euler's formula for a square-based pyramid.
exam.tip: Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 applies to all convex polyhedra.

exam.q: A solid is made of 1cm cubes. The plan is a 2x2 square. The front elevation is a 2x2 square. What is the maximum number of cubes used?
model: A 2x2x2 cube arrangement would satisfy this.
exam.tip: Visualise the 'bounding box' created by the elevations.

exam.q: Explain why a cylinder is not a polyhedron.
model: A polyhedron must have only flat faces and straight edges.
A cylinder has a curved surface.
exam.tip: Use the precise definitions of faces and edges.

exam.q: Draw the net of a triangular prism with a right-angled triangle base (3cm, 4cm, 5cm) and length 10cm.
model: Two right-angled triangles (3, 4, 5) attached to the 10x3 or 10x4 rectangle.
Correct orientation so edges match when folded.
exam.tip: Check that the sides of the triangles match the widths of the rectangles they will meet.

exam.q: A shape has 12 edges and 8 vertices. Name the shape.
exam.tip: Memorise the properties of common solids like the cube and tetrahedron.

exam.q: On isometric paper, draw a cuboid with dimensions 3 units by 2 units by 4 units.
model: Width lines are 3 units at 30 degrees.
Depth lines are 2 units at 30 degrees.
All parallel edges are drawn correctly.
exam.tip: Count the gaps between dots, not the dots themselves.

worked.q: An object is made from 5 centimetre cubes. The front elevation shows a 'T' shape (3 across the top, 1 in the middle below). The side elevation is a single column of 2 cubes. Draw the plan.
steps: Analyze the front: There are 3 cubes in the top layer and 1 in the bottom layer.
Analyze the side: The side view is 1 cube wide and 2 cubes high. This means the object is only 1 cube deep.
Combine: The object is a flat 'T' shape made of 4 cubes, but the question says 5 cubes.
Re-evaluate: If there are 5 cubes, one must be hidden. Since the side elevation is only 1 wide, the 5th cube must be directly behind one of the others.
However, if the side elevation is 1 wide, there can be no 'depth'. Check the question constraints. If the side elevation is 1 wide, the plan must be a 3x1 row.

Wait, if the plan is a 3x1 row, that only accounts for the 3 cubes on the top layer. The 4th is below. The 5th must be behind one of the top ones, making the side elevation 2 wide? No, the side elevation is 1 wide. Therefore, the 5th cube must be hidden in the front view (e.g., behind the middle cube).
Plan: A 3x1 rectangle if the 5th cube is hidden behind the middle one.

worked.q: Calculate the number of vertices on a dodecahedron using the fact it has 12 pentagonal faces.
steps: Each face is a pentagon, so it has 5 edges. 12 faces * 5 edges = 60 edges.
Each edge is shared by 2 faces, so E = 60 / 2 = 30.
We know F = 12.
Use Euler's Formula: V - E + F = 2.
